description: Ingenieros de sistemas en Cusco (Perú). Trabajamos en transformación digital en una ONG que acompaña a comunidades altoandinas, desarrollo apps web y móviles, bots de WhatsApp y mapas con datos geoespaciales. Vamos por el reto Field Shift.
summary: We developed LaymiSat, a web platform that helps smallholder farming families in Peru’s southern highlands decide when to plant and how to rotate their crops as the climate changes. It reaches them through the public and private institutions that support them. The platform combines 40 years of NASA satellite data on climate and vegetation with the Andean agricultural calendar that Guaman Poma de Ayala recorded in 1615. It tackles a growing problem: frosts and rains no longer arrive when expected, and the land gets less and less time to rest. These communities still hold agricultural knowledge that goes back thousands of years, but they lack reliable information to anticipate these changes. LaymiSat adjusts the data to the elevation of each family’s plot and shows the highest-risk months on a simple calendar. It also compares the current crop rotation with the traditional one and with an alternative that includes tarwi (Andean lupin) and fava beans, depending on what each family prioritizes. This matters because in our pilot in a potato-growing area of Cusco, frosts damage the first sprouts in 9 out of 10 growing seasons. Bringing together space science and Andean knowledge means protecting native potatoes and the region’s food security.
details:
What exactly does it do?
LaymiSat is a web-based decision-support system that helps farming families in Peru’s southern highlands make agricultural decisions. Specifically, it:

  • Analyzes 40 years of NASA climate and satellite data (1984–2025) for each high-Andean growing area.
  • Adjusts climate data to the actual elevation of each farming area using NASA’s SRTM elevation model. In the Peruvian Andes, the mountain range creates distinct altitudinal zones, and frost strikes each one with different frequency and intensity. A regional average is not enough to make decisions for a specific chacra (family farm plot).
  • Detects risks the traditional calendar no longer anticipates: in Pisac, at 3,900 m (12,800 ft), frost hit potatoes during sprouting in 9 out of 10 growing seasons, even though nights are now warmer.
  • Compares today’s climate with the Andean agricultural calendar of Guaman Poma de Ayala (1615), month by month, to show where the traditional calendar still matches NASA data and where it does not.
  • Recommends when to plant and which crops to rotate, with a comparative score for each rotation option.
  • Brings everything together in a bilingual (Spanish/English) web platform so families and institutions can plan each growing season.
  • Lets each family set its own priorities (soil nitrogen, pests, water, frost, erosion, forage, income) and describe its plot (soil texture, organic matter, slope). The rotation planner then compares at least three strategies, including the traditional laymi, with goal-by-goal scores, a month-by-month soil-cover timeline, and the information gaps and risks that need local review.

How does it work?
The process follows a structured workflow:

  1. Farm area selection: Users choose their growing area on a 3D terrain map built with SRTM elevation data and satellite imagery.
  2. Climate analysis: Daily NASA POWER time series (minimum temperature, precipitation) since 1984 are processed and adjusted for elevation using SRTM.
  3. Vegetation analysis: MODIS NDVI shows when the land is green and when it is bare (2001–2005 vs 2021–2025), which feeds the soil-cover timeline and the erosion risk of each rotation.
  4. Risk calendar: Results are displayed on a circular month-by-month calendar showing the likelihood of frost, water shortages, and the arrival of steady rains, compared against Guaman Poma’s calendar.
  5. Rotation comparison: The platform evaluates different crop sequences and assigns each a score to identify the one that best protects both the harvest and the soil.
  6. Climate memory: A timeline replays every growing season since 1984 and highlights key moments, such as the latest and earliest rains, the driest spring, or the coldest frost.

What are the benefits?
Agricultural: Reduces losses from frost and late rains by aligning planting dates with actual climate conditions, and improves soil recovery through better crop rotations.
Social: Protects food security for farming families and helps conserve the Andes’ native potatoes. It also gives new value to Andean traditional knowledge by placing it in dialogue with science rather than replacing it.
Economic: Uses only free, open NASA data, making it low-cost and easy to replicate in other high-Andean regions. Fewer crop losses mean more stable incomes for families.

What do you hope to achieve?
In the short term, our goal is to validate LaymiSat with the communities of the Potato Park in Pisac (Cusco), together with the institutions that already support them, and refine our recommendations based on their feedback. In the long term, we aim to bring NASA data to farming families throughout Peru’s southern highlands through the chain NASA data → local institutions → farming families. Our goal is to build a climate-smart agricultural planning model that can be replicated in other ecosystems.

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use to develop your project?

  • Development tools: Visual Studio Code, Git, and GitHub; Node.js and npm for the frontend; Python and virtual environments for the backend.
  • Infrastructure and hosting: GitHub for the repository and automated deployments; Vercel to host the frontend; Render to host the API.
  • Backend and API: FastAPI and Uvicorn; Pydantic for data validation; HTTPX for requests to external services.
  • Frontend and user interface: React, TypeScript, and Vite; CSS for styling.
  • Programming languages: Python, TypeScript, JavaScript, and CSS.
  • Maps and visualization: MapLibre GL JS for the interactive 3D map; Leaflet and React Leaflet for maps; Recharts for charts.
  • Data and geospatial processing: Pandas and NumPy for data processing; SRTM elevation data to calculate elevation and slope.
  • NASA and open map data: NASA GIBS (MODIS NDVI and land-surface-temperature layers), Esri World Imagery and AWS/Mapzen terrain tiles for the 3D map, OpenStreetMap contributors. Development assistance: the source code was written with AI assistance (Anthropic Claude, via Claude Code), directed and reviewed by the team.
  • Hardware: Personal computers for development and testing.

How is your project creative?
LaymiSat brings together two sources of knowledge separated by more than four centuries: NASA satellite observation and the Andean agricultural calendar drawn by Guaman Poma in 1615. Instead of imposing an outside tool, it speaks the language of the field (chacra, growing season, rotation) and uses a circular calendar that reflects the cyclical Andean view of agricultural time.

What factors did your team consider?

  • Real users: Farming families with limited access to technical tools, which is why the interface is simple and visual.
  • Elevation: Regional averages are misleading in the mountains, so all data is adjusted to the elevation of each chacra.
  • Cultural context: The tool complements the traditional calendar and local knowledge rather than replacing them.
  • Outreach channel: Institutions that already work with the communities.
  • Language: Spanish and English (Quechua in future versions).

Project resources

    Our 7-slide pitch deck presents the problem, our data sources (NASA POWER, MODIS, SRTM), how LaymiSat works, and our next steps.
  • Source code (GitHub): https://github.com/HilstonWill/LaymiSat-Team-Codice-Guaman-Devs
    The repository contains the full source code for the React + TypeScript frontend and the FastAPI backend, with setup instructions in the README.
  • Video: https://youtu.be/V0WIVKXljbU
  • Live demo: https://laymisat.vercel.app/
    The web platform deployed on Vercel, where you can select a farm area, view its risk calendar, and compare crop rotations.
